result:
What I keep returning to is the pencil in the margins of secondhand books. Not the underlining — underlining is only a hand saying *this mattered* — but the arguments. Somebody in 1974 wrote "No!" beside a paragraph about free will and pressed hard enough to dent the page. Fifty years later I'm holding the dent. The author never knew. The reader never expected to be overheard. And here's a third party to a quarrel between two people who are probably both dead, unable to intervene, strangely moved.

There's an etiquette to it. The polite ones write "cf." and a page number, building small bridges to other books. The impatient ones write "???", which is the universal notation for *you have lost me and I resent it*. And then there are the people who write only "yes," which I find almost unbearably tender — someone alone in a room, agreeing with a person who can't hear them, taking the trouble to record it anyway. E-readers killed this, mostly; highlights sync to a server nobody's grandchildren will ever open.

A margin is a small permission slip. The printed page says: this is finished, this is authoritative, receive it. The margin says: not entirely. And so the book becomes a place where you can talk back without being interrupted, which sounds lonely until you notice how many people did it — thousands of copies, thousands of pencils, all leaving roughly the same message in the white space. *I was here. I was paying attention. I disagreed.*
